# Conclusion

This study asked whether a human's emotional state, as measured through
FER and HRV, can be predicted above chance from a plant's
electrophysiological signal alone. A multimodal pilot study with 15
participants was conducted, combining heart rate variability and facial
expression recognition into proxy indicators of arousal and valence, with
ambient CO~2~ recorded alongside. The plant signal was evaluated against
these indicators since no self-reported ground truth was collected.

The answer to the study's main question is a qualified yes. The
qualification is twofold: the effect is modest across all three targets,
and it is not equally pronounced across affective dimensions. The latter
should not be read as evidence about the dimensions themselves, since
valence and arousal were operationalized through proxies of unequal
quality, a facial expression model on the one hand and a single HRV
measure on the other. Valence classification produced the clearest result
(macro-F1 = 0.42, permutation p = 0.005), recognizing all three classes
with comparable reliability. The five-class emotion label likewise
reached significance (p = 0.015), but a macro-F1 of 0.21 across five
classes lies close to the uniform-chance expectation of approximately
0.20 and should not be read as substantive support, notwithstanding an
accuracy of 42% driven by the dominant neutral class. Arousal prediction,
resting solely on HRV, did not reach conventional significance
(p = 0.055). **H1 is therefore supported for valence, only nominally for
the crossed emotion label, and not for arousal.**

Feature importance was dominated by shape: the winning valence model
ranked Hjorth mobility and complexity highest, and the amplitude
descriptors behind them entered only in their session-normalized form.
This suggests that the model captures genuine signal dynamics rather than
session-specific baseline drift, an interpretation reinforced by the fact
that session normalization improved performance in most model-target
combinations, though conditional on the band-limited measurement chain
discussed above.

The secondary analysis tested the most plausible alternative explanation
for the valence finding, that ambient CO~2~ rather than the plant tracked
the participant's breathing and thus their emotional state. It does not
hold: the plant--valence association survives controlling for CO~2~
almost unchanged at both the raw and the within-session level, while the
plant--CO~2~ coupling itself appears to be largely a between-session,
room-level effect. **The data therefore provide no support for H2,**
which given the sample size should be read as absence of evidence rather
than as evidence of absence.

These findings must be read against several structural limitations. All
results are validated only against proxy labels; the sample is small,
single-cohort, and recorded on a single day; the fixed stimulus order
leaves session time as an unresolved confound; and no sham or shielding
control rules out electromagnetic artifacts. Future work should
prioritize a larger cohort with self-assessment ratings and directly
recorded respiration to strengthen the arousal axis, and should replicate
the present design across a broader population to determine whether the
weak but statistically robust valence signal reflects a reproducible
phenomenon.
